title: Chapter 83 – The Second-Rank Beast
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The old boar is wounded, and that is the only reason the plan has a chance.

Jian crouches on a shelf of frozen rock at the top of the upper meadow and studies the tracks. It is the morning after the vine. The sun is a pale coin behind cloud. Snow lies in a clean white sheet to the edge of the pines, scored by the rout of yesterday: a hundred cloven prints, churned and trampled, and among them one that is not like the others. It is the size of a dinner plate. It sinks to the ankle even in packed snow. Beside it, every ten paces, lies a dark spatter, almost black against the white.

"Blood," says Zhao Yao.

"Old." Jian rubs a flake between finger and thumb. "Two days. It is not fresh enough to be a wound from the rout. Something hurt it before the others ran."

"You can tell that?"

"I can tell that it has dried at the edges." He wipes his hand on his knee. "Pebble can tell the rest."

The pangolin, on his shoulder, is quiet. It has not spoken since dawn, not even in feelings, and the silence worries him more than the tracks. He lays a hand against its scales and sends a question down the bond. Where?

The answer is slow, cold and tight. Upstream. Under rock. Near water. Large. A pause. Hurt. Angry. Thread.

Thread?

In the throat. Same as the others. The scales prickle against his palm. Bigger. Older. Tighter.

He does not tell the others that part.

* * *

The team has changed overnight.

Feng cannot walk. Wei Chen has set the leg and bound it in jade splints, and he lies in the warm cleft by the black pool, under a cloak, with a bone-white face and his sword across his knees. He has refused to be carried back to the gate. "I will keep the vine," he said, to nobody, and nobody argued. Wei Chen sits on a rock beside him, with his indigo hood back and the bamboo case across his lap, ostensibly keeping watch. Jian suspects he is keeping something else.

That leaves three.

They stand at the edge of the meadow in the cold gray light: a girl of seventeen with a white spear, a boy of fourteen with a borrowed one, and a man of twenty-one with a stick. It is not a hunting party. It is not even a good argument for one.

"The slip said four," says Tan Ruyan.

"The slip said a leader of the eighth layer or above," says Jian. "It did not say anything about the others."

"It said a team of four."

"Wei Chen has stayed with my brother by right of injury. Under the Hall's regulations, a member who is hurt in the line of duty counts as present." He has read the rule. He read it twice, on the eve of the mission, with Ma Bao's candle. "We are four. One is lying down."

She looks at him a long moment. Then, unexpectedly, she smiles, a real one, brief and crooked. "You read everything."

"It passes the time."

"It does." She turns the spear in her hands. "I have been thinking about the marrow."

"Yes."

"It is the leader's right. You know that. I have said I would take it." Her eyes are level. "I have also watched you break a ford with a stick. I have no idea how you did it. I do not think I want to know. But I understand that you have a way of seeing things, and I have a spear, and the old male is a Foundation beast." A pause. "If I fight him alone, I die. If you plan and I fight, we may both live. I am not stupid, Lin Jian. I do not care for fairness. I care for living."

"Then we agree."

"We agree on that. We do not agree on the marrow." She tilts her head. "A boar of the second rank has two long bones in each foreleg. A vial each. The slip promised the leader one. It said nothing of the other."

She has already worked it out.

"The Pill Hall's writ," says Jian, carefully, "entitles the Hall to a share of any alchemical part taken by an expedition it supplies. Bai wrote that into the warrant. It says one long bone."

"One."

"One."

"I could challenge the writ."

"You could. It would cost a week." He meets her gaze. "Or you could take the first vial as leader, and I could take the second as the Hall's, and neither of us would have to explain to Overseer Han why we are both short."

Tan Ruyan is silent for the length of three breaths. The wind moves in the pines. In the distance, up the long white meadow, a crow, the first he has seen in nine days, rises from a tree and flaps heavily away.

"If your plan works," she says, "you have the second. If it does not, neither of us has anything." She holds out her hand. "Agreed?"

He takes it. Her fingers are hard and dry and warm.

"Agreed."

* * *

The plan is simple, because there is nothing else it can be.

Jian lays it out on the snow with a stick, in lines and circles, while the others watch. It has three parts. He has been working at it since the middle of the night, lying in the dark of the cleft with a pangolin on his chest and Feng's slow breathing in his ear.

One. Where he lives. The tracks lead upstream, along a narrow gorge where the main stream falls in a series of drops from a ledge a hundred feet above. Pebble has been there in the night, in a manner of speaking; it sent a long thin trail of feeling down the bond until Jian had it like a map in his mind. At the head of the gorge, behind a screen of boulders, there is a wallow: a hollow dug into the bank beneath an overhanging cliff, warm with spring water and steaming in the cold. The old boar is in it. It has been there since the rout.

Two. What he wants. The boar is hurt. It will not leave the wallow for any reason but one: food. A beast of the second rank eats flesh, and it has eaten none in two days. The meadow is full of its dead kin, the rout's casualties, half-buried in snow. Jian proposes to move three of them. A trail of fresh meat, laid down the gorge to the mouth of the wallow, and a fourth, the best, laid under the cliff.

Three. What is above him.

He draws a line. It is a long horizontal slab, the thickness of a door, jutting from the cliff like a shelf twenty feet above the wallow. He has not seen it. Pebble has. It is a single piece of gray rock, the length of a cart, held to the cliff by a seam so thin that it is almost not a seam at all.

"There is a crack," he says. "Behind the slab. It runs from the top of the cliff to the base. If it is struck from above at the right place with the right note, the slab will drop."

"On the boar."

"On the place he will be standing. Under the cliff, on the meat."

Zhao Yao frowns. "You mean to strike a cliff from above. We do not have a rope long enough."

"We do not need one. I strike it from the side." Jian draws a small cross on the line. "Here. A narrow ledge, forty paces across the gorge. I stand there. The slab is a drum. If I hit the wall behind me with the right force, the note runs through the seam to the slab. It does the rest."

"Hollow Echo," says Tan Ruyan.

He had not said the name. She says it as one says the name of a flower. He looks at her.

"I have heard of it," she says. "It is a Yellow technique, a pulse that returns from cavities. It is not common in the Court. It is common in Qingshi." Her smile is thin. "Merchants use it to find the hollow in a wall."

"Yes."

"I will not tell Wei Chen."

"Thank you."

"I will tell him you struck a cliff with a stick. It is the truth." She stands and brushes snow from her knees. "Where do you want me?"

"At the mouth of the wallow, with the spear." He draws a last mark. "The boar will come for the meat. You will be the thing that stops it from going past. You will hold it, for the length of three breaths, on the right spot. Not more."

"Three breaths."

"I need three. The slab needs one."

"And if it takes four?"

"Then I will be wrong," says Jian, "and you will have to run."

She looks at him gravely. "I would rather you were not wrong."

"So would I."

* * *

The meat goes down the gorge at mid-morning, dragged on a cloak by three people, leaving a ribbon of red on the snow.

It is the worst part of the day. Jian has done grim things in his short time in the Sect, but this is the first time he has been a butcher. The boars are heavy and the cold has stiffened them. Zhao Yao works silent and gray, with his lips pressed together. Tan Ruyan does not flinch. They lay three carcasses at intervals along the gorge and the fourth, a young sow, at the head of the gully beneath the cliff, in the open, on a patch of bare gravel that the wind has scoured clean.

The wallow lies thirty paces beyond. Jian can smell it from here: a thick, hot, rank odor of mud and musk and old blood.

There.

He takes his place on the ledge. It is a narrow strip of rock, hardly wider than his feet, forty paces across the gorge and a man's height above the stream. The cliff rises behind him, wet and black. Across the gap, the slab hangs over the gravel like the lid of a box.

Pebble.

Here, comes the warm, steady answer. The pangolin has curled itself against the base of his neck. He feels its heartbeat through the scales.

Where is the seam?

Two hands left. Down. There. The bond flares with a clear, precise, almost painful image: a thread of dark in the gray, no wider than a hair, running down the face of the rock. Strike. Now?

Not yet.

He waits.

The gorge is very quiet. The stream drips. High above, a snow-bound pine creaks. Tan Ruyan crouches in the shadow of a boulder at the mouth of the gully, her white spear across her knees. Zhao Yao is behind her, farther back, with the second spear and a coil of rope.

The first sign is the smell.

It rolls down the gorge from the wallow like a hot wind: a stink of blood and rot and something sweet and wrong underneath. Then comes the sound. A deep wet rumbling, rising slowly, like a pot beginning to boil. Then the earth begins to shake.

He sees it come out of the boulders.

It is bigger than he expected. It is bigger than anything he has seen alive. It stands as high as a cart, wide as a door, gray-bristled, with shoulders like a bull's and tusks like the curved blades of scythes, each one as long as his arm. Its eyes are small and red. Its jaw hangs open on a gout of foam. Along its left flank, from shoulder to hip, runs a long deep gash, black with dried blood and yellow with pus, and in the gash something moves.

It is not a wound, he thinks. It is a door.

It lurches toward the sow. It has not seen them. It does not look up. It puts its head down to the meat and begins to tear.

And Tan Ruyan steps out.

* * *

She does it beautifully.

She comes round the boulder at a run, with the white spear leveled, and the yellow light running up its shaft. She drives the point into the ground at the old boar's feet. The earth answers. A wall of packed stone and gravel heaves up out of the scoured patch, a hand high, a knee high, a waist high, and closes round the beast's forelegs like a trap.

The boar roars. The sound hits Jian across the gorge like a fist.

It heaves. The gravel wall cracks. Tan Ruyan sets her feet and pours more light into the spear, and the wall holds, and the beast lunges against it with its whole weight, and the wall cracks again.

One.

She is shaking. Sweat runs down her face. She has not lost her poise, but the poise has become something else, a hard grim thing like a clenched fist. She is an eighth-layer cultivator holding a second-rank beast by the legs.

Two.

The boar throws its head up. For the first time, it sees her. The red eyes fix on her face, and the great jaws gape, and a tusk comes round in a long sweeping arc at the height of her chest.

Three.

Jian brings the stick down on the wall.

He does it with both hands, the way Hu taught him. Not hard. Hard is for hammers. He puts the stick against the wet black stone at the place where Pebble showed him, a hand's width left of his hip, and he listens. He lets his breath go out, all of it, and feels for the note.

It is a low, deep, round note. Like a bell under water.

He strikes.

The sound goes into the rock. For a heartbeat, nothing happens. The echo comes back from the cliff face, from the slab, from the long dark crack behind it, and he feels it in his bones like a second heart. It is exactly the sound he heard on the fortieth landing, in the hollow beneath the post. It is not the same. But it is the same family. And as the note runs through the stone, the Seal below his navel answers.

It happens without his leave.

A flash of green light passes across his chest. It is thin and pale and brief, no brighter than a firefly. But in the dim gorge it is like a lamp lit in a cellar. It shines through the cloth of his tunic, outlines his ribs, and rises in a faint luminous curl toward his throat.

No. No. Not now.

He claps his left hand over his chest and presses. The light flickers and dies. The Seal, resentful, sinks back into the dark. But in the instant it shone, he is aware of a head turning, high above, on the rim of the gorge: a long calm figure in an indigo hood, standing against the sky.

Wei Chen is looking down.

* * *

The slab falls.

It does not fall at once. It comes away from the cliff with a long groaning crack, like a tree splitting, and for a second hangs in the air, a cart-sized sheet of gray stone with a trail of dust. Then it drops. It drops a full twenty feet onto the gravel beneath the cliff, onto the sow, onto the boar's hind half, with a sound like the end of the world.

The earth jumps. Tan Ruyan is thrown backward. Zhao Yao, behind her, goes down in a spray of gravel. The gorge fills with a roaring cloud of dust, and a great shriek goes up, thin and shrill and terrible, and stops.

Silence.

Jian stands on the ledge with his hand on his chest and his legs trembling and the stick still in his fingers. The dust settles slowly. The sun is behind the cloud, and the light is gray and flat. Below him the slab lies across the gravel at a slant, and from beneath it, a long gray flank sticks out. One tusk. A rear leg, twitching. Then not twitching.

Dead.

It is not a clean kill. The slab has broken the beast's back and pinned its hindquarters, but the front half is free, and as he watches, one huge foreleg scrapes feebly at the gravel. A low rattling breath comes out of the throat.

Tan Ruyan is already up. She has retrieved her spear. She walks across the broken ground with her face white and her teeth set, and stops beside the boar's head. The red eye rolls up at her. She says something, very low, in the old dialect of Qingshi. It might be a prayer.

She drives the spear into the base of the skull.

The beast shudders once, and is still.

Wei Chen comes down the gorge slowly, picking his way over the broken stone.

He has left Feng in the warm cleft with a fire and a promise. His hood is back and his long calm face is turned up toward the new raw scar on the cliff where the slab came away. He stops at the edge of the gravel, a few paces from the carcass. He looks at the dead boar, at the fallen slab, at the broken wall of earth where Tan Ruyan held. Last, and longest, he looks at the ledge across the gorge.

"A fine fall," he says.

"Thank you, Senior Brother," says Jian.

"I did not say it was well done. I said it was a fine fall. A slab of that size, with a seam so thin, struck from forty paces by a youth of twenty-one with a stick." The heavy-lidded eyes lower to Jian's face. "I saw a light."

Jian says nothing. His heart is going quietly and steadily, like a clock.

"Green," says Wei Chen. "Very faint. In the chest. A little before the slab came down." He holds the boy's gaze. "It might have been the sun on the ice. There was a gap in the cloud."

"There was, Senior Brother."

"There was a gap," says Wei Chen, thoughtfully. "At about the time the slab came away. It is possible that a sunbeam passed through the gorge and struck a patch of frost on your tunic." His mouth does not move. "I am an honest man. If I am asked, I will say that I saw a flash. I will say I cannot be sure what caused it. I do not like to lie to the Hall. I find I do not like to be asked."

"Yes, Senior Brother."

"You will not make me ask."

"No."

"Good." The Inner disciple looks once more at the boar, at the slab, at the golden gleam in the vial. Then he turns to go. "The Medicine Valley owes you a debt, Junior. The beasts of the upper valley were driven mad, and you have shown me how. I would not like it said that the Hall was ungrateful." He lifts a hand, in farewell, and halts. "One thing more. Whatever you are hiding, hide it better. The valley has other eyes than mine."

He goes up the gorge without looking back. Jian watches the indigo cloak between the pines until it is gone.

* * *

They harvest the marrow in the gray afternoon, with the bone knife and the stag-horn tongs.

It is a slow, messy business. Jian has never done it. He has only the Pill Hall's page to go on: Cut the forelegs at the second joint. Split the long bone. Draw the marrow with a hollow reed into a vial of cold jade. Do not touch it with iron. Zhao Yao holds the leg. Tan Ruyan holds the knife. Jian holds the reed.

The marrow is a thick, luminous, faintly golden paste, and it smells of copper and earth. It goes into the vial in a slow, slick thread. It glows. When the vial is full, it sits in his palm warm as a living thing and heavy as a coin, and a low note runs up his arm, the same note that sang in the pill.

Level 2. Second-rank beast. One of five.

He stoppers it. He does not look at the other. Tan Ruyan fills hers, and caps it, and slips it into her satchel with the speed of a person who does not want to be seen enjoying it. They look at each other across the broken carcass.

"Thank you," she says.

"Thank the slab."

"I will." Her voice is steady. "I do not think I will tell the Court who aimed it."

"I would be obliged."

"You may be." She wipes the knife on the snow. "But I want it understood that I know. I know you are a Pill Hall apprentice with a pangolin and a stick. I know you strike a cliff and it falls. I know the Seal..." She stops. Her eyes are very bright. "Never mind. I know that if I were the Master of the Hall of Enforcement, I would want to have a long, quiet talk with you. And I know that I am not." A pause. "That is all I mean to say."

"It is more than enough."

"Good." She picks up her spear. "Then I will go and tell Wei Chen the vials are full."

She goes. Zhao Yao sits on a rock with his head in his hands.

Jian is alone with the carcass.

He kneels by the great gray head. The red eye is dull now. The huge jaws hang open. And under the stiff bristles at the throat, just where the skin folds, as he knew it would be, a line of black.

He pulls the bristles back with the tip of the knife.

It is a thread. It is thicker than the ones on the smaller boars, as thick as a bowstring, and it is wound three times round the neck. It is not stuck in the flesh. It has been sewn in, with tiny regular stitches, in the manner of a surgeon closing a wound, and at the knot beneath the jaw the tail of it lies loose, like the end of a ribbon.

It is not black. In the light, it shines faintly red.

It was not driven mad by fear, he thinks, slowly. It was driven. Like the others. Like a team of oxen, with a rein.

He looks at the stitches. They are very small. They are very neat. He has seen the like only once before: in the hem of a dead man's cloak in the Garden, in the sleeve of a woman who sat a quiet vigil in a hospital tent, in the corner of a Deacon's register. A fine, even, patient hand.

The same hand.

He touches the knot, and the thread parts.

It is a clean cut, as if a blade had passed through it. The two ends curl away from each other like the legs of a dying insect. And in the instant they separate, the knot beneath the jaw, a small hard tangle of black, no larger than a barley grain, turns over in the bristles and lies face up.

He knows it.

It has three loops, one pulled tight and two slack, tied off in a figure that no ordinary hand would choose. He has seen it once before. It was under the rail of a cot in Reed Courtyard, on the night of the Register, a gray knot of the same thread, tucked in the join of the wood where no one would think to look. He had left it. He had thought it a watcher's mark, a thing that said this one is being counted.

Not a watcher.

He kneels in the blood-stained gravel with the severed thread across his palm and understands that the knot under his bed and the knot in the boar's throat are not the work of two people. They are the same hand, the same patient evening's work, the same tie. A man who ties the same knot in a courtyard of sleeping boys and in the neck of a beast in a high snowbound valley is a man who can be in both places.

Or a man who has sent something to be there for him.

Above the gorge, among the pines, a crow calls once and stops.
